title: Does Romans 8:28 Mean Everything Happens for a Reason?
subtitle: Paul wrote it from inside a groaning creation, to a church that would soon face the sword. What it promises, what it never said, and why it is no explanation to hand the grieving.

sections.title: The Sentence on the Sympathy Card
sections.body:
Romans 8:28 lives a long way from Romans 8. It's lettered on kitchen walls and stitched into pillows, written inside sympathy cards, and underlined in Bibles that have been through a divorce and a diagnosis, usually in the familiar wording that all things work together for good.

The people who love this verse aren't naive, and they deserve better than the eye-roll it sometimes gets. Many of them learned it the hard way. They buried someone, or lost the work they had built a life around, or kept watch beside a hospital bed, and this sentence was one of the things that held. They hear in it that the worst thing will not be the last thing, and that nothing, not even this, has slipped out of God's hands. They are hearing something true.

The skeptic has a point too, and it deserves to be granted in full. We have also used this verse to get out of the room. We've handed it to the newly bereaved as though it explained the death, recited it to hurry people through grief, and used it to keep quiet about harm that should have been named and stopped. Somewhere along the way it merged with a sentence that isn't in the Bible at all: everything happens for a reason. A skeptic who hears that at a child's funeral is left with two options: either the reason is monstrous or the sentence is empty. That skeptic is taking the words more seriously than we did when we said them.

The answer isn't to take the verse off the wall. It's to read it where Paul put it, in the middle of a passage full of groaning.

sections.title: Spoken From Inside the Groaning
sections.body:
Paul wrote Romans around AD 57, most likely from Corinth, to house churches of Jews and Gentiles in Rome he had never visited (Romans 1:13). Some of them already knew what imperial power could do. Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2), and Priscilla and Aquila, forced out by that order, were back with a church meeting in their house by the time Paul wrote (Romans 16:3-5).

The paragraph around verse 28 says more than a wall hanging has room for. Paul starts from “our present sufferings” (Romans 8:18) and names three groanings in a row. The whole creation, subjected to futility and bound to decay, “has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until the present time” (Romans 8:22). Believers groan too, even with the Spirit's firstfruits, as they wait for “the redemption of our bodies” (Romans 8:23). And the Spirit groans, because “we do not know how we ought to pray, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words” (Romans 8:26). None of this is optimism.

Then comes the sentence everyone knows: “And we know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose” (Romans 8:28). Its “we know” answers the “we do not know” two verses earlier. Paul doesn't claim to know what to pray, or why the creation groans as it does, or when it will stop. He claims one thing, and he says it from inside the groaning.

If that wording differs from the one you know, there's an honest reason. A few important early manuscripts name God outright as the one at work and most don't, and the shorter wording can be read either way, so some translations say all things work together for good while others, like the Berean Standard Bible quoted here, make God the subject. Either way, the verses on both sides concern the Spirit's prayer and God's purpose. Nothing in this paragraph works on its own.

sections.title: The Good Paul Had in Mind
sections.body:
Paul doesn't leave the good undefined. The next sentence names it: “For those God foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29). The good is likeness to Jesus, worked out in a family where he is the eldest brother. It isn't comfort, or success, or the answer someone was pleading for in a waiting room. And the likeness includes the part of his life nobody frames, since a few verses earlier Paul calls believers co-heirs with Christ “if indeed we suffer with Him, so that we may also be glorified with Him” (Romans 8:17).

Christians have argued for centuries over what foreknew and predestined mean here, a disagreement that divides faithful churches but not the faith. Every side agrees on where the chain is headed: to “glorified” (Romans 8:30), a verb Paul puts in the past tense, as though it were already done.

Then he names what might tear them away from all this: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall trouble or distress or persecution or famine or nakedness or danger or sword?” (Romans 8:35). He calls none of it good. He quotes Psalm 44, a lament from faithful people who suffered anyway and told God so: “we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered” (Psalm 44:22). The next line of that psalm is “Wake up, O Lord! Why are You sleeping?” (Psalm 44:23). Only then does Paul write “in all these things we are more than conquerors” (Romans 8:37). He sets an unanswered lament inside his most confident paragraph and doesn't apologize for it.

The first hearers would need every line. Less than a decade later, after the great fire of AD 64, Nero blamed Rome's Christians and put many of them to death. Whatever this verse promised the church in Rome, it didn't promise that the sword would stay sheathed. It promised them a love the sword couldn't reach.

sections.title: What It Promises, and What It Never Said
sections.body:
Read in its place, the verse promises less than we've hung on it, and more. It doesn't say the tragedy was good. Working all things together for good is a different claim from calling all things good, and Paul only makes the first. The clearest proof is in the chapter itself, in the God “who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). God worked the greatest good in history through the worst thing ever done, and the crucifixion never stopped being a murder. Peter's sermon at Pentecost holds both together: Jesus was “delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge,” and put to death “by the hands of the lawless” (Acts 2:23). Whatever you believe about how God governs a world with evil in it, this verse won't let you call the cancer good, or the abuse, or the accident.

Nor does it promise that you'll be shown the reason. Paul's word for the Christian posture is waiting, since “hope that is seen is no hope at all” (Romans 8:24). Joseph was eventually shown how God meant for good what his brothers meant for evil (Genesis 50:20), but only after decades. Job never learned what the reader of his book is told in its first two chapters.

And the good it promises isn't the good you would have chosen. The prosperity preacher who turns this verse into a guarantee of health and money, and the political Christian, right or left, who waves “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31) over an election, are making the same trade. Each swaps the good Paul named, likeness to a crucified Son, for a good that can be seen and counted. It's an easy trade, and none of us is above making it.

What the verse does promise is harder and better. Nothing that has happened to you, including this, is outside God's work, and nothing in all creation “will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:39).

sections.title: How to Pray It, and When to Keep Quiet
sections.body:
Pray the verse the way Paul said it: from inside the groaning, after admitting you don't know what to pray, with Psalm 44 close at hand. It's a confession of trust, not a verdict on an event. It can be said through tears, and on the days you only half believe it, the church can say it for you, because the “we know” was always plural.

This verse should never be handed to someone in fresh grief as an explanation. It doesn't explain the loss; it never says why. Offered as an explanation, it tells the person in front of you that their loss was God's good idea, which Paul never said, and it asks them to finish grieving before they've started. The same letter says to “weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15), and Jesus, who knew he was about to raise Lazarus, wept when he saw Mary weeping (John 11:33-35). If the one who knew the ending wept first, the rest of us can sit in silence a long while before we quote anything. Those of us whose work is to say something at the bedside need that warning most.

If you're the one grieving, you don't have to make this verse work tonight. The Spirit intercedes when we can't find words (Romans 8:26-27). Tell someone who loves you how heavy it is, and if the dark has become more than you can carry, tell a doctor, a counselor, or a pastor today.

Living the verse doesn't mean lying down in front of harm, either. The man who wrote it escaped Damascus in a basket (Acts 9:25) and appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11). Trusting God to work in all things has never meant staying in danger or keeping quiet about abuse.

Romans 8:28 doesn't answer the first question grief asks, the question why. It answers a later and lonelier one, whether anyone is still holding us, and Paul says yes with his eyes open, to a church that would soon be counted as sheep for the slaughter. He doesn't lift them out of the groaning to say it. The verse lives between the groaning and the glory, and for now, so do we.
